l: Orontes of Indian race, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a corpse [a perfect man] The god in Clarus told Syrians consulting the oracle that the giant corpse found in the old channel of the Orontes was Orontes of Indian race. The text connects this identification with the claim that India produced mortals earlier or larger than other regions.

l: India, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: India is described as producing mortals earlier or larger and unusual, large beasts; it has leopard-colored camels and martiora, called manslayer by Greeks, while remote areas may hold animals unlike Greece's.

l: market-place of Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_located_on right of the river’s course [in a northerly direction] The market-place of Megalopolis lies to the north, on the right of the Helisson’s course. It contains precincts and a stone temple to Lycæan Zeus, Philip’s portico, Hermes Acacesius’ temple, public offices, the Myropolis and Aristandreum porticoes, a temple of Zeus Soter, and the statue of Polybius.

l: Nymphs, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Nymphs throw Rhea’s afterbirth into Lymax, inspire prophetic people, and are linked to Mount Ida through the second Herophile’s mother and to Herophile’s tomb.

l: Friendly Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Friendly Zeus has a temple inside the precincts; his Polycletus-made statue resembles Dionysus, wearing buskins and holding a cup and thyrsus topped by an eagle.

l: the temple of the Great Goddesses and of Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: contains Aphrodite [Aphrodite’s statue is inside] The temple contains statues made by Damophon, including a wooden Hermes and a mostly wooden Aphrodite. Old wooden statues of Hera, Apollo, and the Muses from Trapezus stand before its entrance.

l: Muses, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Muses are a group first honored on Helicon by Ephialtes and Otus. Thought by the sons of Aloeus to be three, Melete, Mneme, and Aoide, they were later established as nine at Thespia by Pierus; they are also brought from Trapezus as old wooden statues and sing at Harmonia’s marriage.

l: the worship of the Great Goddesses, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: imitates the Eleusinian Mysteries Callignotus, Mentas, Sosigenes, and Polus are said to have first instituted the worship of the Great Goddesses at Megalopolis. The worship is described as an imitation of the Eleusinian Mysteries.

l: the temple of the Great Goddesses, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: contains the rites of the Great Goddesses [a large temple was built for them] A large temple is built for several gods, including Hermes, Apollo, Athene, Poseidon, the Sun surnamed Soter, and Hercules. The rites of the Great Goddesses are celebrated there.

l: the rites of the Great Goddesses, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The rites of the Great Goddesses are celebrated in a large temple built for several gods within the precincts.

l: the temple of Proserpine, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Proserpine stands right of the temple of the Great Goddesses, contains an eight-foot stone statue with fillets at its base, and restricts men’s entry to once yearly while women may always enter.

l: theatre, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A remarkable theatre in Greece, across the river in the city and facing south, contains a perennial spring.

l: council-chamber, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Thersilium, near the theatre, is a council-chamber built by its namesake builder for 10,000 Arcadians.

l: racecourse, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: extends_towards theatre [in one direction] A racecourse lay beyond the temple of Aphrodite. One part extended toward the theatre, where there was a spring sacred to Dionysus, and another part was associated with a temple of Dionysus said to have been struck by lightning two generations earlier.

l: hill, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_situated east [towards the east] A hill lay toward the east, with a temple of the Huntress Artemis on it and precincts sacred to the Huntress Artemis on its right. Another temple stood under the hill, containing Asclepius as a boy and a seated Apollo.

l: Hades, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Hades is the setting for the painting’s scenes of the dead and their punishments. Eurynomus is described as a demon in Hades who eats the flesh of the dead.

l: deity, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: introduces_changes changes [habitually] The deity is said to favor change and to reduce everything to subjection, bringing formerly strong and prosperous places such as Megalopolis, Mycenæ, Nineveh, Thebes, Babylon, and Tiryns to ruin or diminished condition.

l: human affairs, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: are fleeting and unstable Human affairs are described as fleeting and unstable, as shown by the rise and decline of cities and by the disappearance or creation of islands.

l: Messene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Messene, destination of roads from Megalopolis, has an unconquered citadel. After Agesilaus declined combat at Sparta, Epaminondas turned to colonizing and restoring sacred Messene, bringing her children back.

l: Maniæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Maniæ is a place on the road from Megalopolis to Messene, about 7 stades from Megalopolis, with a temple of goddesses; its name is thought a title of the Eumenides.

l: Ace, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ace is a place contiguous with Finger’s tomb and Maniæ, where Orestes was said to be healed of madness and containing a temple to the Eumenides.

l: Orestes’s madness, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_caused_by the pursuit of Orestes by the Furies of Clytæmnestra [in the account of his madness after matricide] Orestes’s madness was said to have begun at Maniæ after the murder of his mother. It was associated with his gnawing off a finger and ended at Ace when the Eumenides appeared white to him.

l: the pursuit of Orestes by the Furies of Clytæmnestra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Furies of Clytæmnestra pursued Orestes before his Areopagus trial, when Perilaus accused him and sought vengeance for Clytæmnestra’s murder.

l: Gatheatas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Gatheatas rises at Gatheæ near Cromi, receives the Carnion, and flows into the Alpheus.

l: temple of Despœna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Despœna, four stades from Acacesium, stands in Despœna’s sacred enclosure, reached from the temple of Artemis the Leader; it contains statues, throne, altars, and a mirror that reflects them clearly but viewers obscurely.

l: Despœna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Despœna, privately named Persephone, is the Arcadians’ most-worshipped god. According to their tradition, she is daughter of Poseidon Hippius and Demeter. Seated before her temple, she holds a sceptre and cist; her mystic rites occur in a nearby Hall and grove, while her private name is withheld from the uninitiated.

l: Belemina, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Belemina, about 20 stades from Phalæsiæ, has a temple of Hermes; Arcadians say it was theirs before Lacedæmonians took it, a disputed claim.

l: Phalanthus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A Spartan, son of Agelaus and grandson of Stymphelus, led the Lacedæmonian colonization of Tarentum under an oracle. After failure, he interpreted his wife’s tears and captured Tarentum; he also survived a shipwreck by reaching shore on a dolphin.

l: Atalanta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Atalanta first wounds the Calydonian boar, earns its head and hide for her prowess, and is represented among the hunters on a temple gable.

l: Tanagra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tanagra is a place with temples to Dionysus, Themis, Aphrodite, Apollo, Artemis, Leto, and Hermes. Its people separate houses from temples, keep temples pure, greatly honor gods, and preserve traditions about Hermes, Corinna, and two kinds of cocks.

l: statues of Despœna and Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The statues of Despœna and Demeter, with their throne and footstool, were made by Damophon from one stone block found within the temple precincts after a dream vision; each was about the size of the statue of the Mother at Athens.

l: Hall of Despœna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_near temple of Despœna [up a little to the right] The Hall of Despœna lies a short ascent to the right of her temple. The Arcadians perform her Mystic rites there and sacrifice victims in abundance.

l: enclosure sacred to Lycæan Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The sacred enclosure on Mount Lycæus forbids entry to men; violators are said not to live more than a year. Throughout the year, men and beasts within it cast no shadows, so hunters cannot see an entering beast’s shadow.

l: the 100 picked men from Oresthasium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The 100 picked men from Oresthasium volunteered for the expedition to Phigalia, fought bravely to the death, fulfilled the oracle, and drove out the Lacedæmonian garrison.

l: Lacedæmonian garrison, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_driven_out_by the 100 picked men from Oresthasium [from Phigalia] The Lacedæmonian garrison at Phigalia engaged the 100 picked men from Oresthasium. It was driven out by them, allowing the Phigalians to recover their native town.

l: capture of Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The capture of Phigalia occurred in the second year of the 30th Olympiad after the Lacedæmonians defeated the Phigalians and besieged their town.

l: flight of the Phigalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a flight [from Phigalia] The flight of the Phigalians occurred after the Lacedæmonians had nearly taken Phigalia by storm. The Phigalians evacuated the town, either on their own initiative or because the Lacedæmonians allowed them to leave under conditions of war.

l: oracle concerning the return to Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Oracle concerning the Phigalians’ return to Phigalia: it denies hope if they return alone, but promises success if they take 100 picked men from Oresthasium, who must be slain in battle.

l: expedition to Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The expedition to Phigalia was undertaken by the 100 picked men from Oresthasium together with the Phigalians' effort to recover their town. The men engaged the Lacedæmonian garrison, died fighting bravely, and fulfilled the oracle.

l: battle at Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: In the battle associated with the recovery of Phigalia, the 100 picked men from Oresthasium fought the Lacedæmonian garrison. All 100 were killed, but they drove out the Spartans and made the return of the Phigalians possible.

l: return of the Phigalians to Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_enabled_by the 100 picked men from Oresthasium [through their death in battle] The Phigalians' return became possible after the 100 picked men from Oresthasium drove out the Lacedæmonian garrison and died in battle. The Phigalians thereby recovered their native town.

l: Arrhachion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Arrhachion, a pancratiast with two earlier Olympia victories, broke an opponent's finger in his final contest, died while being throttled, and was proclaimed victor, receiving wild olive.

l: statue of Arrhachion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: An antique stone statue of Arrhachion, depicted as a pancratiast, stands in the market-place of Phigalia; it has close-set feet and hands near the buttocks, while its inscription has been obliterated.

l: Olympic victories of Arrhachion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Arrhachion won twice at Olympia before the 54th through umpire equity and merit; in his final contest, the people of Elis awarded him victory after his death.

l: opponent of Arrhachion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a antagonist [the only one remaining in the contest] Arrhachion's last opponent seized him with his feet and tightly grappled his neck with his arms. Arrhachion broke the opponent's finger, while the opponent throttled Arrhachion and then fainted from the pain in his finger.

l: Creugas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Creugas, a boxer from Epidamnus, died when Damoxenus struck under his ribs and tore out his bowels; afterward Argives awarded him Nemea victory and erected a statue in Argos.

l: Damoxenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Damoxenus, a Syracusan boxer, breaks his one-strike agreement with Creugas, kills him by tearing out his bowels, and is driven from the course.

l: boxing match between Creugas and Damoxenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A boxing match between Creugas and Damoxenus ends fatally after they agree to one strike each. Creugas strikes first; Damoxenus then tears out Creugas’s bowels, and the Argives judge that he violated the agreement by giving several blows.

l: Lymax, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lymax is a river flowing by Phigalia and winding into the Neda near hot baths; the Phigalians name it for Lymata, Rhea’s purifications.

l: Neda, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Neda, a notably winding river, rises on Cerausius, receives Lymax near Eurynome, and flows to the sea, navigable there for small craft.

l: temple of Eurynome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Eurynome stands at the Lymax-Neda confluence in rough, cypress-surrounded country. Difficult to access and holy since remote antiquity, it stays shut except its annual festival day, when Phigalians sacrifice publicly and privately.

l: Eurynome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Eurynome is identified by the Phigalians as a title of Artemis, while Antiquarians describe her as Oceanus’s daughter who joined Thetis in receiving Hephæstus; her statue is woman above and fish below, chained in gold.

l: Cotilius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_located 40 stades from Phigalia [about] Cotilius is a mountain about 40 stades from Phigalia and part of the surrounding landscape. It contains Bassae, the temple of Apollo the Helper, the place called Cotilum, and a spring whose water soon disappears into the ground.

l: Elaion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Elaion is a mountain about 30 stades from Phigalia, containing a cave sacred to Black Demeter.

l: temple of Apollo the Helper, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Apollo the Helper stands at Bassae on Cotilius, with a stone roof. Noted for its beautiful stone and neat structure, it ranks among the finest Peloponnesian temples after Tegea and was built by Ictinus.

l: cave of Black Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The cave of Black Demeter on Mount Elaion near Phigalia is sacred from Demeter’s stay, surrounded by oaks and a warm bubbling spring.

l: Onatas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Onatas, son of Mico, was a sculptor of Ægina. He made notable brazen statues of Demeter for Phigalia and Apollo for Pergamus, and, with Calynthus, votive offerings of the Tarentines. His Demeter followed an ancient painting or copy, perhaps aided by a dream.

l: the oracle's response, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The oracle's response identifies Black Demeter’s recess and directs the people of Phigalia to seek relief from famine there, warning of cannibalism unless they appease Demeter through public libations and restored divine honours.

l: wooden statue of Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A wooden statue of Demeter, made by the people of Phigalia and placed in a cave, showed her seated on a rock with a woman’s body, mare’s head and mane, and monsters around her head. Called Black Demeter for its black dress, it wore a foot-length tunic and held a dolphin and dove. It later burned; its maker and circumstances were unrecorded.

l: brazen statue of Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Onatas made a bronze statue of Demeter for Phigalia from a painting or copy; falling cave-roof stones later completely destroyed it.

l: famine at Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_caused_by Demeter [when Demeter’s fruits of the earth were blighted] Famine followed the neglect of Demeter’s festivals and sacrifices after the earlier statue was destroyed. The people of Phigalia consulted the oracle, restored Demeter’s honours, and then resumed worship and sacrifices.

l: annual sacrifice to Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: At Phigalia, the annual sacrifice to Demeter is conducted by a priestess and the youngest Sacrificing Priest. Fruit, honeycombs, and unworked greasy wool are placed on the altar before the cave, covered with oil, and offered without an animal.

l: Evander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Evander, an Arcadian from Pallantium and son of Hermes by a Nymph, excels in counsel and war, then leads Arcadians to found Rome near the river Tiber.

l: tax exemption of Pallantium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The tax exemption of Pallantium was granted by the elder Antonine when he made Pallantium a town. The privilege made it free and exempt from taxation.

l: Mauri, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Mauri are the most important independent Libyan tribe, nomadic and formidable because men and wives ride horses. The elder Antonine drives them from all their territory into remote regions, including Mount Atlas and its neighbourhood.

l: Libyans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Libyans are described as early colonists of Sardinia under Sardus, coexisting with its original inhabitants and lacking cities. They later returned in greater force, defeated Greeks, drove Trojans into the mountains, and, after disputes with Carthaginians over spoil, settled in mountainous areas as Balari.

l: Mauri war with Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: War between the Mauri and Rome begins with Mauri hostilities; the elder Antonine drives them from their territory, forcing retreat toward Mount Atlas after Roman defeat.

l: inheritance law favoring the Emperor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A law governing Roman citizens whose sons were reckoned as Greeks directed inheritances away from sons toward unrelated people or the Emperor; Antonine later allowed property to be left to those sons.

l: Antonine's philanthropy, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: permits_inheritance_by sons [rather than preserving the revenue-raising law] Antonine's philanthropy included allowing eligible citizens to leave property to their sons rather than increasing the Emperor's wealth. He also gave money to needy Greeks and barbarians and supported magnificent works in Greece, Ionia, Carthage, and Syria.

l: Pius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Pius was the title the Romans gave the elder Antonine because of the honour he paid to the gods. The text says he might also justly have been called the elder Cyrus or Father of mankind.

l: son Antonine, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The son Antonine succeeds the elder Antonine, fights the Germans, and subdues the Sauromatae after their iniquitous war.

l: Germans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Germans are Europe’s most numerous and warlike barbarians; Antonine’s son fought against them.

l: Sauromatae, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Sauromatae commenced an iniquitous war and were subdued by the son Antonine.

l: war between the son Antonine and the Germans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a war [between the son Antonine and the Germans] The war between the son Antonine and the Germans involved the son Antonine fighting against the Germans, who were described as the most numerous and warlike barbarians in Europe.

l: Sauromatae's war with Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: An iniquitous war begun by the Sauromatae against Rome, ultimately subdued by the son Antonine.

l: the Mound, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Mound marks Megalopolis, Tegea, and Pallantium; roads from it lead toward the Pallantium and Manthuric plains.

l: the Eurotas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Eurotas rises near Asea, joins the Alpheus, flows underground, disappears into a cavity, and reemerges in Laconia.

l: great temple of Athene Alea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The great temple of Athene Alea at Tegea surpassed Peloponnese temples in beauty and size. Built by Scopas the Parian, it combined Doric first-row, Corinthian second-row, and Ionic outer pillars. Its gables showed the Calydonian boar hunt and the combat between Telephus and Achilles.

l: statue of Athene at Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The statue of Athene at Tegea, called Hippia by the Manthurii and Alea by other Greeks and Peloponnesians, was taken from the Manthurii; Æsculapius and Hygiea stand beside it, made by Scopas in Pentelican marble.

l: Tegeans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tegeans, Arcadians, shared wars against Ilium and Persians and battle at Dipæa, then became first Arcadians to defeat and capture most opposing Lacedæmonians.

l: Pirithous, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Pirithous, praised for friendship with Theseus, sits with him on an enchanted rock and indignantly regards his useless sword during their venture.

l: Telephus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Telephus, son of Auge and Hercules, is born to Auge, exposed on Mount Parthenium as a boy, and survives by being suckled and brought up by a doe, according to tradition.

l: Athene Alea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Athene Alea is an ancient ivory statue by Endœus, carried away by Emperor Augustus after victory over Antony and allies, then displayed in Augustus’s Forum at Rome.

l: custom of carrying off votive offerings and statues, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A long-established custom among Greeks and barbarians, it involves victors carrying off votive offerings and statues from conquered nations, illustrated from Ilium through Cyzicus and Proconnesus.

l: Capaneus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a son of Hipponous Capaneus, the son of Hipponous, made a violent attack on the walls of Thebes at Electris. He was said to have been struck by lightning there.

l: victory of Augustus over Antony and his allies, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: After defeating Antony and allied Arcadians except Mantineans, Augustus removed Athene Alea's ancient statue and the Calydonian boar's tusks.

l: temple of Athene at Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Athene at Tegea is a place containing notable votive and sacred objects: the Calydonian boar’s hide, rusty fetters of Lacedæmonian captives, Athene’s bed, Auge’s effigy, Marpessa’s armour, statues of the Muses and Mnemosyne, and an altar said to be made by Melampus.

l: Marpessa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Marpessa, the Widow from Tegea and once priestess of Athene, excelled Tegean women in daring against the Lacedæmonians.

l: temple of Athene Poliatis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Athene Poliatis at Tegea, called the temple of Protection by the Tegeans, is entered yearly by its priest and is said to guard Tegea through Medusa’s hair granted to Cepheus by Athene.

l: market-place at Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The brick-like market-place in Tegea contains temples, statues, pillars, an altar, and the tombs of Tegeates and Mæra.

l: Brick Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Brick Aphrodite is worshipped in a temple in Tegea’s market-place, alongside a stone statue of the goddess.

l: Iasius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Iasius, son of Eleuther, won a horse-race at Olympia when Hercules the Theban established the Olympian games. He is commemorated by a pillar statue in the Tegea market-place, touching a horse with his left hand and holding a palm branch.

l: Ares Gynæcothœnas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ares Gynæcothœnas is a statue of Ares on a pillar in Tegea’s market-place, named for women’s separate sacrifice after their victory over the Lacedæmonians.

l: Laconian war, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: included women of Tegea [who took up arms] During the Laconian war, at the first invasion led by Charillus, the women took up arms and ambushed the Lacedæmonians under the hill later called Phylactris. The women helped cause the Lacedæmonian rout.

l: women's sacrifice to Ares, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: After victory over the Lacedæmonians, women of Tegea privately and independently sacrificed to Ares, excluded men from the flesh, and gave Ares the name “Women’s Feast.”

l: temple of Ilithyia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Ilithyia stands in Tegea’s market-place, containing a kneeling statue called Auge; tradition says Auge gave birth to a son where it stands.

l: birth of Telephus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: occurred_at temple of Ilithyia [on the spot where the temple now stands] One tradition places the birth of Telephus at the spot where the temple of Ilithyia now stands, as Auge fell on her knees while being led away. Another tradition says that Auge gave birth to him without her father’s knowledge.

l: cavalry of the Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_the_best_in Greece After Philopœmen was chosen commander, he made the cavalry of the Achæans the best cavalry in Greece. Under his leadership it defeated the cavalry of the Ætolians and the men of Elis at the river Larisus.

l: battle at the river Larisus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Battle at the river Larisus: Achæans and allies fought Elis and supporting Ætolians; Philopœmen killed cavalry commander Demophantus, then routed the Ætolian and Elean cavalry.

l: Celts, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Celts are barbarians whose expeditions and invasions extend beyond their borders. Under Cambaules, their first expedition reaches Thrace but goes no farther. In a second expedition with infantry and cavalry, they invade Macedonia, Thrace, Pæonia, and Greece, defeat Macedonians after Ptolemy falls, outrage Thessaly, and advance near Magnesia and Phthiotis. Crossing the ocean and then the Sperchius despite destroyed bridges, they invade Greece but suffer heavy losses at Delphi, compounded by winter, rocks, panic, and starvation. The surviving forces in Macedonia and Thrace return to Asia Minor the following year.

l: Machanidas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a tyrant [of Lacedæmon] Machanidas rose to power in Lacedæmon and led its forces against the Achæans. After pursuing the fleeing Achæan light-armed troops at Mantinea, he encountered Philopœmen and was slain by him.

l: Pythian games, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Pythian games began with singing a hymn in honour of Apollo and later included musical, athletic, chariot, and horse-racing contests. Over time, the games discontinued singing to the pipes, introduced contests such as the race in armour and the pancratium for boys, and awarded victors a laurel crown.

l: freedom, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Freedom and immunity from taxation were granted to the Elateans by the Romans for their successful resistance to Taxilus and the barbarians from Pontus.

l: Manius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: commands Romans [at Thermopylæ] Manius and the Romans defeated Antiochus and the Syrians at Thermopylæ. He was willing to receive the Lacedæmonian fugitives, but Philopœmen opposed the proposal before the Council; after Manius departed, Philopœmen allowed the fugitives to return to Sparta.

l: Dinocrates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Dinocrates, leader of the wealthy Messenians, urged and used poison to kill Philopœmen, then committed suicide after Lycortas and the popular party punished those responsible.

l: popular party, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Messene’s popular party sought to save Philopœmen, called him Greece’s father, then joined Lycortas’s forces and saw his murderers executed.

l: Cleombrotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a king [of the Lacedæmonians] Cleombrotus, king of the Lacedæmonians, turned aside to Ambrosus in Phocis, passed through after killing Chæreas and his men, and reached Leuctra. He fell in the battle against the Thebans.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: serve_under_pay_of Persia [50,000 Greeks] The Greeks were defended or aided by figures including Miltiades, Leonidas, Themistocles, Conon, Epaminondas, Leosthenes, and Aratus. Leosthenes brought 50,000 Greeks who had served for pay under Persia safely back to Greece by ship.

l: Battle of Marathon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Battle of Marathon yielded spoils shared with the Platæans and dedicated by the Athenians as firstfruits. Arimnestus commanded the Platæans; a tenth of the spoils funded Acropolis statues of Athene, Apollo, Miltiades, heroes, and other figures, made by Phidias.

l: Battle of Thermopylæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Battle of Thermopylæ was a Greek victory over the Galati: narrow, rocky terrain worsened the poorly armoured, inexperienced Galati’s defeat and disorderly retreat, causing many deaths; 40 Greeks were killed.

l: inscription on Philopœmen at Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: commemorates Philopœmen The inscription says that Philopœmen's fame and glory spread throughout Greece. It commemorates his wisdom in council, bravery in the field, eminence as a cavalry leader, victories over two Spartan tyrants, abolition of slavery, and defense of his country's freedom.

l: Apollo Aguieus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Apollo Aguieus, linked to punishment for neglecting Leto and Scephrus’s death, receives four Tegean statues; at his festival, the people honor Scephrus.

l: people of Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The people of Tegea recount Apollo and Artemis punishing those who neglected Leto, Tegeates’ sons migrating to Crete, rites for Scephrus, four tribal Apollo Aguieus statues, annual Zeus Clarius festivals, and victories over the Lacedæmonians.

l: Scephrus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tegeates’ son Scephrus privately spoke with Apollo at Tegea; his brother Limon killed him in mistaken suspicion, and Delphi ordered mourning.

l: Limon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: kills Scephrus [in a mistaken suspicion] Limon, the brother of Scephrus and son of Tegeates, mistakenly believed that Scephrus was making an accusation against him and slew him. Artemis immediately killed Limon with an arrow, and his pursuit is reenacted by the priestess of Artemis at Tegea.

l: festival of Apollo Aguieus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: honors Scephrus [according to the people of Tegea] At the festival of Apollo Aguieus, the people of Tegea pay honors to Scephrus. The priestess of Artemis pursues someone during the festival, acting out Artemis’s pursuit of Limon.

l: Cithæron, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cithæron, king and ruler of Platæa, famed for ingenuity, advised Zeus to deceive Hera with a dressed wooden statue and wagon.

l: Platæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Platæans are thought to be the original inhabitants of their land, named for Platæa, probably daughter of Asopus. In early history they were ruled by kingship. They fought alongside the Athenians after Xerxes’ landing, helped defeat Mardonius on their own soil, repulsed the barbarian, and received spoil for a temple to Arean Athene after the Battle of Marathon. Twice driven from Platæa and twice restored, they returned to Athens after the first capture and later occupied Platæa with a strong garrison. Their religious life includes temples to Arean Athene and Eleusinian Demeter, offerings to Apollo, restoration of Gargaphia, and the smaller Dædala procession to Mount Cithæron.

l: capture of Platæa by the Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: was_carried_out_by Lacedæmonians [during the Peloponnesian war] The Lacedæmonians captured Platæa during the Peloponnesian war after besieging and enclosing it with a double wall, which prevented the inhabitants from leaving.

l: Cadmea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cadmea, built by Cadmus, grows into lower Thebes’ citadel and is joined to the lower town by Amphion and Zethus.

l: Bœotarch, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Epaminondas’s period of office as Bœotarch expired, and the law imposed death as the penalty for continuing in office beyond the proper time. He disregarded the law, continued as Bœotarch, and was later acquitted because none of the judges would sentence him.

l: second capture of Platæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Three years after Leuctra, under Asteus at Athens, Thebans captured Platæa again while inhabitants were outside, ordering those inside to leave.

l: destruction of Platæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: was_carried_out_by Thebans [after the second capture; the town was razed except for its temples] After the second capture, the Thebans razed Platæa entirely except for its temples. There was no sack, and the Athenians again received the Platæans.

l: restoration of Platæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: was_carried_out_by Philip [after his victory at Chæronea] Philip restored Platæa after his victory at Chæronea and the introduction of his garrison into Thebes.

l: Mount Cithæron, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Mount Cithæron is a sacred mountain of Zeus of Cithæron, holding ruins, a tomb, and traditions of Pentheus and Œdipus. It received the Dædala procession and altar; below its summit, Sphragidion was linked to Nymphs’ prophecies.

l: Actæon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Actæon, son of Aristæus, is a hunter associated with a fawn, hound, and deerskin. After hunting, he slept near a spring and saw Artemis bathing; one account says she dressed him in deerskin so his dogs devoured him, while another attributes their madness without her intervention. At Orchomenus, his spectre harmed the land until his found remains were buried and annual funeral rites established.

l: Semele, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Semele, intended spouse of Actæon in one account, is Dionysus’s mother by Zeus; Thebans say her statue and sepulchre stand in the temple of Lysian Dionysus.

l: Œdipus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Œdipus is a person, son of Laius, exposed at birth on Mount Cithaeron after his ankles were pierced and later brought up in Corinth and near the Isthmus. Though the exact place of his exposure is unknown, an oracle led Laius to expose him, and Œdipus was fated to kill his father and marry his mother. He learned an oracle given to Cadmus in a dream, brought a force from Corinth, and slew the Sphinx. At the crossroads on the road to Phocis, he unwittingly slew Laius, then washed his father’s blood at the Well of Œdipus. His patricide and incest brought later woes. He was father of Polynices in the account naming Euryganea as the children’s mother; Polynices left Thebes during his lifetime, and Œdipus died before his return.

l: altar of Zeus Eleutherius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The white-stone altar of Zeus Eleutherius stands near the common tomb of the Greeks at Platæa, where the Eleutheria includes heavy-armored races before it.

l: Eleutheria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Eleutheria is a festival at Platæa celebrated every fifth year, culminating in competitors running in heavy armor before the altar of Zeus Eleutherius for chief prizes.

l: temple of Hera, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Hera in Platæa is a place notable for its size and beautiful statues; at its entrance is Rhea carrying the swaddled stone to Cronos, followed by standing and seated Heras.

l: wooden statue (bride of Zeus), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The wooden statue was dressed as a young bride, placed in a wagon, and presented as Platæa in Zeus's false marriage plan. Hera tore its clothes when she discovered that it was only a wooden image.

l: Dædala, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Dædala was a festival commemorating the reconciliation of Hera and Zeus, named from dædala, an old term for statues; it unfolded as a smaller Platæan celebration and a great festival for all Bœotia.

l: oak-coppice near Alalcomenæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: An oak-coppice near Alalcomenæ contains Bœotian oaks reputed for the finest roots; at the smaller Dædala, Platæans used a crow-selected tree to carve a wooden image.

l: Alalcomenæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Alalcomenae is a small village at a low mountain’s foot, said named for Alalcomeneus or Alalcomenia; its plain holds Athene’s temple and the small torrent Triton.

l: dædalum, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a wooden image [carved from the tree selected by the crows] A dædalum was the wooden image carved for the festival. The text says that statues were formerly called dædala and suggests that this usage preceded the time of Dædalus the Athenian.

l: great festival of Dædala, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The great festival of Dædala, held for all Bœotia every sixth year after restoration, joined Coronæans, Thespians, Tanagræans, Chæroneans, Orchomenians, Lebadeans, and later Thebans. For the smaller festival, communities provided fourteen wooden statues yearly, decorated them, carried them from the Asopus to Mount Cithæron, and burned them with animal sacrifices.

l: Thespians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Thespians are Bœotians who possessed Ceressus, colonized Sardinia in Iolaus’s expedition, and honored Eros above all gods, holding a festival at Helicon’s grove. Regretting ill-will toward the Thebans, they fled their city to Ceressus, where Epaminondas captured them. Their city had Eros images, Black Aphrodite’s temple, theatre, marketplace, and other monuments.

l: Orchomenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Orchomenians were inhabitants of Orchomenian country, a broader people from whom the Phlegyas separated, also called Minyæ and distinguished from Arcadian Minyæ. Ruled by Erginus, then Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, they fought Hercules and the Thebans and were defeated, went to Troy and Ionia, were expelled by Thebans, and restored by Philip son of Amyntas.

l: Asopus river, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The decorated wooden image was placed on a wagon at the Asopus. The participating communities then drew lots for the procession and drove their wagons from the Asopus to the top of Mount Cithæron.

l: altar on Mount Cithæron, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: An altar on the top of Mount Cithæron, built of square wooden pieces and firewood, receives sacrifices to Hera and Zeus; smaller private offerings, images, and the altar itself are consumed in a very large fire.

l: temple to Arean Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple to Arean Athene at Platæa, built from spoil given by the Athenians after the Battle of Marathon, contains the goddess's statue. Its vestibule holds paintings by Polygnotus and Onatas, while the statue's base bears an effigy of Arimnestus.

l: Arean Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Arean Athene is represented at Platæa by a nearly life-sized wooden statue that is gilt over, with the head, fingers, and toes made of Pentelican marble.

l: statue of Arean Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The statue of Arean Athene at Platæa is a nearly Acropolis-sized work by Phidias, wooden and gilt over, with Pentelican-marble head, fingers, and toes.

l: Polygnotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Polygnotus is a Thasian painter, son of Aglaophon, identified by Simonides as the artist of scenes from the capture of Ilium. His painting in The Lounge ranges from Troy’s destruction and the Greeks’ return to Odysseus’ descent to Hades. It depicts Epeus breaking Troy’s walls, the Wooden Horse, Ajax’s oath concerning Cassandra, Neoptolemus killing Trojan men, Phrontis, wounded warriors, and many named figures. On the left, it shows Acheron, Charon, punishment and honor in Hades, Theseus and Pirithous, Eurynomus, and Ocnus making rope while a she-ass consumes it, apparently satirizing Ocnus’ wife. Further figures include the daughters of Pandareus, Antilochus, Agamemnon, Achilles, Patroclus, Phocus, Iaseus, Actæon, Orpheus, Thamyris, and Marsyas. Polygnotus appears to draw on Homer, Lescheos, the Minyad, and Archilochus, while also adding or inventing names and details not found in those accounts. The painting culminates in a deliberate-looking gathering of enemies of Odysseus and a depiction of Tantalus following Archilochus.

l: fountain Gargaphia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Fountain Gargaphia was fouled by Mardonius and Persian cavalry, then its water was made pure again by Platæans.

l: river Oeroe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Oeroe is a river on the route from Platæa to Thebes, said in local tradition to be Asopus’s daughter.

l: Asopus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a_boundary_between Platæa and Thebes [districts] The Asopus lies near the river Oeroe and is still the boundary between the districts of Platæa and Thebes.

l: Cadmus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cadmus is a leader and founder associated with a Phoenician army, Cadmea, Thebes, dragon’s teeth, and a journey directed by an oracle. He received an oracle at Delphi, travelled toward Phocis following a marked cow, and settled where it lay down, erecting an altar and statue of Athene. He invaded the land, defeated the Hyantes, allowed submissive Aones to mix with the Phoenicians, and built Cadmea. He was said to slay a dragon at a well and sow its teeth near Thebes’ gates, producing armed men. He chose Echion as son-in-law, married Aphrodite and Ares, migrated to the Illyrians and Enchelians, and was succeeded by Polydorus.

l: Laius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Laius, son of Labdacus, was entrusted to Lycus after his father died and later restored to the kingdom. Warned that a son by Jocasta would kill him, he exposed Oedipus, who nevertheless killed him. He also had sons by mistresses and was said to father the Sphinx.

l: Amphion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Amphion, described as Antiope’s and Acestor’s son and Zethus’s brother, is a Cretan famed for lyre, music, and singing. After receiving a lyre from Hermes and discovering nete, he and Zethus invade Thebes, defeat Lycus, and join the lower town to Cadmea. Later punished in Hades, he is buried near Zethus.

l: Zethus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_brother_of Amphion [sons of Antiope] Zethus is buried with Amphion in a low mound of earth. His sepulchre was involved in the ritual by which people from Tithorea attempted to improve the fertility of their land.

l: Antiope, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Antiope, driven mad after Dirce’s cruel death attributed to Dionysus’s anger, wanders Greece, is cured and married by Phocus, and is buried with him.

l: Thamyris, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Thamyris is a blind, dejected figure depicted near Pelias, with thick hair and beard, handling a broken lyre whose strings are torn apart.

l: the Minyad, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Minyad is a poem recounting Theseus and Pirithous entering Charon’s boat alive, among accounts of Hades and its horrors.

l: Euryganea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Hyperphas’s daughter Euryganea is said to mother Oedipus’s four children and is depicted dejected by her sons’ quarrels.

l: Jocasta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Jocasta marries Laius, bears Oedipus, whose foretold killing of Laius precedes Jocasta's later marriage to Oedipus.

l: Polynices, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Polynices, Eteocles’s brother, leaves Thebes fearing his father’s curses, goes to Argos, and marries Adrastus’s daughter. Recalled after Oedipus’s death, he quarrels with Eteocles and returns to exile. With an army from Adrastus, he fights Eteocles; both die. Antigone brings his corpse to Eteocles’s funeral pile, and his son Thersander inherits the Theban line.

l: Eteocles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Eteocles is a king of Andreis, described variously as son of Oedipus, Andreus through Euippe, or the river Cephisus, and called Cephisiades in some poems. As king he retained the country’s name, founded the tribes Cephisias and Eteoclea, granted a village to Almus, and was credited with first sacrificing to and establishing worship of three Graces. After Oedipus’s death, he quarrelled with his brother Polynices; they fought and killed each other. Accounts differ on whether succession went to his son Laodamas or Almus’s posterity, as he died without male progeny.

l: Menoeceus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Menoeceus, Creon’s son, voluntarily kills himself as Delphi’s oracle directs when Polynices and his Argive army approach Thebes; his tomb stands near gate Neistis.

l: Glisas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Glisas is ruins beyond and left of Teumessus, where the Epigoni and Thebans fought a later battle ending in Theban defeat; above it stands Highest with Highest Zeus’s temple and altar, beside Thermodon.

l: Oedipus's patricide and incest, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Oedipus was fated to kill his father, Laius, and to marry his mother, Jocasta, after doing so. Homer says that the gods soon made the relationship publicly known; Pausanias uses this to argue that Oedipus and Jocasta did not have children together.

l: Coronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Coronea, given to Thersander through Haliartus and Coronus, has marketplace altars of Hermes Epimelius and the Winds, and a temple with an ancient Hera statue by Pythodorus; Mount Libethrium and Mount Laphystium lie nearby.

l: Phocian War, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: During the Phocian War, Thebans set fire to the Temple of Apollo at Abæ while Phocian fugitives who had been defeated in battle were seeking refuge there.

l: Sulla, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Sulla is a person and military leader in a war with Mithridates. He begins the war, invades Bœotia, and punishes the Thebans despite their attempt to renew friendship with Rome by taking half of Thebais. He takes votive offerings from Olympia, Epidaurus, and Delphi for his troops, gives half of Thebais to the gods in return, and offers a statue of Dionysus. He also removes an old ivory Athene statue, attacks Greek cities, and erects a trophy at Chæronea after defeating Taxilus and Mithridates’ army. At life’s end, he is afflicted with lice disease.

l: Mithridates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Mithridates was opposed to Rome in a war that the Thebans joined, apparently because of their friendship with the Athenian people.

l: Thebais, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_returned_to Thebans [by the favour of the Romans] Sulla took half of Thebais from the Thebans, giving it to the gods in return for votive offerings collected from Olympia, Epidaurus, and Delphi. The Thebans later recovered the land through the favor of the Romans.

l: war with Mithridates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Thebans joined Mithridates in his war against Rome, apparently out of friendship for the Athenian people. Sulla's invasion of Bœotia during this war caused the Thebans to panic and seek renewed friendship with Rome.

l: restoration of Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The restoration of Thebes followed the expulsion of the Thebans by Alexander. Cassander carried it out with assistance from the Athenians, Messenians, and Arcadians of Megalopolis.

l: Potniæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Potniæ is a ruined place about 10 stades from Thebes, with a grove of Demeter and Proserpine, statues by the river, rites involving sucking pigs, a temple of Dionysus Ægobolus, and a well believed to make local horses mad.

l: grove of Cabirian Demeter and Proserpine, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A grove about twenty-five stades from gate Neistis, dedicated to Demeter and Proserpine, accessible only to initiated persons.

l: Dionysus Ægobolus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a Goat-killer [epithet] Dionysus Ægobolus, or Goat-killer, had a temple at Potniæ. After the people killed his priest while drunk, a pestilence came upon them, and Delphi instructed them to sacrifice a grown boy; not many years later, the god is said to have accepted a goat instead.

l: seven gates of Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Seven gates within the old walls of Thebes, Electris, Prœtisis, Neiste, Crenæa, Highest, Ogygia, and Homolois, each receives explanations or traditions for its name.

l: Electris, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_named_after Electra [the sister of Cadmus] Electris was named after Electra, the sister of Cadmus. The road from Platæa entered Thebes through this gate, and it was said to be the place where Capaneus was struck by lightning while attacking the walls.

l: Homolois, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Homolois, the most recently named of seven gates, was named after Homole because Thebans returning with Thersander entered Thebes through it.

l: Homole, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a Thessalian mountain [the most fertile and well-watered of all the Thessalian mountains] Homole was described as the most fertile and well-watered of the Thessalian mountains. The Thebans who had fled after being defeated by the Argives occupied it before Thersander restored them to Thebes.

l: war between the Argives and the Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A war between the Argives and Thebans over the sons of Œdipus, regarded as more memorable than the Eleusinian-Athenian war, moved from the Peloponnese into Bœotia and included battles at Ismenius and Glisas.

l: war between the Thebans and the Minyæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The conflict followed the imposition of the yearly tax after Clymenus's murder. The Minyæ suffered great reverses when Hercules caused the tax to be remitted, and Erginus then made peace with Hercules.

l: battle of Ismenius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: At Ismenius, Thebans flee after initial defeat, then kill attackers from Thebes, destroy the army except Adrastus, and suffer heavy losses.

l: Ismenius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ismenius was the place where the Argives and Thebans fought the battle in which the Thebans ultimately destroyed the Peloponnesian army.

l: Cadmean victory, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A Cadmean victory is a victory won with heavy losses to the victors, named by the Thebans after their costly victory at Ismenius.

l: Epigoni, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Epigoni was a Greek army led by Thersander. Not many years after the war involving Adrastus, it marched against Thebes, strengthened by recruits from Argolis, Messenia, Arcadia, Corinth, and Megara, and defeated the Thebans at Glisas.

l: battle of Glisas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The battle of Glisas was a sharply contested fight between Epigoni and Thebans, ending with Theban defeat, flight with Laodamas, and blockade.

l: Thebais, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Thebais is an epic poem about war between the Argives and Thebans, specifically the Epigoni’s campaign against Thebes; considered later than the Iliad and Odyssey, it includes Periclymenus killing Parthenopæus.

l: sons of Œdipus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The sons of Œdipus fight single combat; Argives and Thebans wage war over them. They have tombs near Thebes, where, during sacrifices, flame and smoke divide.

l: hill sacred to Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ismenius is a hill sacred to Apollo, right of the gates; Apollo and the river share its name.

l: Ismenius River, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ismenius is a river flowing by Apollo’s sacred hill, sharing its name with the hill and god; before Apollo’s son Ismenius was born, it may have been called Ladon.

l: Temple of Ismenian Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a temple [of Ismenian Apollo] The Temple of Ismenian Apollo has stone statues of Athene and Hermes at its entrance, called gods of the Vestibule; the Hermes is by Phidias and the Athene by Scopas. Inside is a cedarwood statue of Apollo attributed to Canachus, and nearby is Manto’s seat, the stone where Manto is said to have sat, along with statues of Henioche and Pyrrha.

l: spring sacred to Ares, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a spring [sacred to Ares and higher than the temple of Apollo Ismenius] A spring said to be sacred to Ares lies somewhat higher than the Temple of Apollo Ismenius. Ares is said to have placed a dragon there to guard it.

l: Caanthus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Caanthus, son of Oceanus and brother of Melia, was sent to find Melia after her carrying off. Finding her with Apollo, he burned Apollo's grove and was killed by Apollo's arrow; his tomb lies near Ares's sacred spring.

l: Melia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a mother of Tenerus and Ismenius [with Apollo as father] Melia is said to have been the daughter of Oceanus and the sister of Caanthus. Apollo had carried her off, and Caanthus found her with Apollo while searching for her.

l: bridal-bed of Alcmena, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A bridal-bed made by Trophonius and Agamedes for Amphitryon’s marriage to Alcmena, later shown among his house’s ruins.

l: temple of Hercules called Champion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Hercules called Champion is dedicated to Hercules and contains white-stone and wooden statues, including works attributed to Xenocritus, Eubius, and Daedalus, later receiving colossal Pentelican-marble statues of Athene and Hercules.

l: Icarus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Icarus, Daedalus’s son, awkwardly overturns his boat and drowns; Hercules finds, recognizes, and buries him, after which an island and nearby sea receive his name.

l: Apollo Spodius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Apollo Spodius, a deity, commands Siphnii to send revenue to Delphi and protects Delphi, telling its inhabitants not to fear. He opposes Celts and Galati through ground-shaking, thunder, lightning, falling rocks, and panic that makes them slaughter one another.

l: Harmonia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Harmonia is said to have made the three ancient wooden statues of Aphrodite as votive offerings, using wood from the gunwales of Cadmus’ ships. She associated their titles with pure love, common sensual love, and the turning of men’s hearts toward lawless passion and unholy deeds.

l: Pronomus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Pronomus is a highly attractive flute-player who discovered a single flute usable for every kind of measure and first played different measures on it. His appearance and movements delighted theatre audiences; his processional song remained in use among Chalcis dwellers at Delos, and the Thebans erected his statue.

l: Pelopidas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Pelopidas was imprisoned by Alexander while visiting him as a personal friend and a friend of the Theban people. He was released after Epaminondas took command of the Theban force.

l: Ambrosus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ambrosus, in Phocis beneath Mount Parnassus opposite Delphi, is traditionally named for the hero Ambrosus. During war against Philip and the Macedonians, Thebans built double walls; it has a small market-place of mostly broken statues and a downhill road to Anticyra.

l: Bœotarchs, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: number seven The Bœotarchs disagreed over whether to engage the Lacedæmonians or prepare for a siege. Their votes were initially divided equally, but Bacchylides, the seventh Bœotarch, returned from Cithæron and voted with Epaminondas, leading them to choose battle.

l: allies of the Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The allies of the Lacedæmonians had previously been dissatisfied with them and showed their hostility during the engagement by giving way wherever the enemy attacked. Some suffered no deaths, while others lost only a few men, unlike the Lacedæmonians.

l: war between the Lacedæmonians and the Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The war began after the Lacedæmonians and the Thebans came into conflict, with the Lacedæmonians attacking the Thebans alongside their allies. The war included the battle at Leuctra, where the Thebans defeated the Lacedæmonians.

l: colonization of Messene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_conducted_by Epaminondas [after Agesilaus declined a combat] The colonization of Messene was undertaken by Epaminondas after he marched against Sparta and Agesilaus declined a combat.

l: Theban allies, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: overrun Laconia The Theban allies overran Laconia and plundered it, scouring the whole country. Their actions induced Epaminondas to take the Thebans back into Bœotia.

l: Iphicrates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Iphicrates, son of Timotheus, commands Athenians and targeteers attacking Epaminondas near Lechæum; after their rout and pursuit toward Athens, he prevents the Athenians from going out to fight.

l: temple of Ammon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Ammon, near Epaminondas’ statue, contains Calamis’ Ammon statue and Pindar’s hymn inscribed by its altar.

l: Thracians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Thracians captured some Thebans and conducted them to Haliartia. The captives were freed by Dionysus and given an opportunity to kill the Thracians in their sleep.

l: temple of Lysian Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Lysian Dionysus stands near the theatre at Prœtis, has a statue said to be Semele, and opens yearly on stated days.

l: temple of Artemis Euclea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Temple containing a statue of Artemis Euclea by Scopas and the burials of Androclea and Alcis; a lion reportedly dedicated by Hercules stands before it, with statues of Apollo Boedromius and Hermes Agoræus nearby.

l: Erginus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Erginus, eldest son of Clymenus and grandson of Presbon, ruled Orchomenus after Clymenus. He led the Minyæ against Thebes and secured a yearly tax, but made peace with Hercules when the citizens were reduced to extremities. Unmarried and childless until old age, he consulted Delphi, married a young wife, and fathered Trophonius and Agamedes.

l: Clymenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Clymenus, son of Presbon and king of Orchomenus, fathered Erginus, Stratius, Arrho, Pyleus, and Azeus; Thebans killed him at Onchestian Poseidon's festival, and Erginus succeeded him.

l: sepulchre of Zethus and Amphion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A low earth mound housing Zethus and Amphion; Tithorea tried moving its soil to Antiope’s tomb for fertility, while Thebans guarded it against blight.

l: Tithorea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tithorea is a place in Phocis, also called Neon, though Bacis calls it Tithorea. Originally the name covered the entire district; local tradition names the nymph Tithorea as its source. About 80 stades from Delphi by Mount Parnassus, it has a theatre, ancient market-place, Athene’s grove and shrine, Antiope and Phocus’s tomb, and water from the Cachales. Its people guard the sepulchre of Zethus and Amphion and seek earth from it for Antiope’s tomb to improve fertility. Its fortunes worsened, and roads lead to Ledon and toward Drymæa through Tithronium.

l: Phocus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Phocus is described both as Ornytion’s son and Sisyphus’s grandson, who finds, cures, marries, and is buried with Antiope, and as Aeacus’s son. In the latter account he crosses from Ægina to Phocis, gains sovereignty, receives Iaseus’s gold-set stone signet-ring, returns to Ægina, and dies through Peleus’s contrivance.

l: Sisyphus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a son of Æolus Sisyphus, the son of Æolus, is shown laboriously rolling a stone up a hill.

l: tomb of Amphion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Amphion’s tomb is near his funeral pile. Stones lying near it in no particular order were said to be the stones that followed Amphion’s music.

l: Orpheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Orpheus is a Thracian poet, described as the son of Pierus, though Greeks supposed him to be the son of Calliope. He excelled earlier poets in arranging poems and wrote verses to Eros for the Lycomidæ’s mysteries. His greatest influence came from being credited with inventing mysteries, purifications, cures, and means of turning away divine wrath. Traditions connect him with Eurydice and attribute his death variously to Thracian women, lightning, or suicide. He does not compete at Delphi because of his solemn relation to mysteries and elevation of soul. At Helicon he appears with Telete and animals listening to his singing; another scene places him on a hill in Proserpine’s grove, holding a harp, touching and leaning against a willow, and dressed Greek rather than Thracian.

l: Tydeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tydeus is slain by Melanippus during the Argive siege of Thebes, then reportedly buried by Mæon beneath three rude stones near Melanippus’s tomb; Athenians claim Lysander bribed him.

l: Well of Œdipus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_named_for Œdipus The Well of Œdipus is near the tomb of Hector and is named for Œdipus’s washing away there the blood from his father’s murder.

l: Teumessus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Teumessus is a place on the high-road, said to have hidden Europa by Zeus; its fox harmed Thebans until it and its pursuing dog became stone, and it has an unstatueed temple of Athene Telchinia.

l: Mycalessus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Mycalessus, a depopulated town near Harma and the sea, was named for the cow that led Cadmus and his army to Thebes and lowed there; it has a temple of Mycalessian Demeter.

l: Mycalessian Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Mycalessian Demeter is a deity with a sea-near Mycalessus temple, entrusted to Idæan Hercules; fruits at her statue remain fresh all year.

l: temple of Mycalessian Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple near the sea at Mycalessus is nightly shut and opened by Hercules; inside, fruits of Autumn at Demeter’s statue remain fresh throughout the year.

l: temple of Artemis at Aulis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Artemis at Aulis contains two stone statues, one with torches and one like an archer. Near its plane-tree well, it is associated with a doe sacrificed for Iphigenia, Homer’s plane-tree remains, and accepting all victims.

l: people of Tanagra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The people of Tanagra inhabit the district around Mycalessus, Harma, and Aulis; they trace their founding to Pœmander and describe Tanagra’s name changing to Graia before returning.

l: Delium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Delium is a place near the sea in Tanagra, containing statues of Artemis and Leto.

l: Pœmander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Pœmander, son of Chæresilaus, founded Tanagra and married Tanagra; his lineage extends through Iasius and Eleuther to Apollo and Æthusa.

l: Tanagra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tanagra, said to be Æolus’s daughter and Pœmander’s wife, or Asopus’s daughter according to Corinna, lived to advanced age, was called Graia, and gave her name to a city before it recovered Tanagra.

l: Corinna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Corinna, the only poetess of Tanagra, composed in Aeolic and defeated Pindar at Thebes; her victory, credited partly to dialect and beauty, was commemorated by a conspicuous tomb and a gymnasium painting.

l: Graia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a name of Tanagra [an earlier name retained for a long period] Graia was the name given to Tanagra because of her exceptionally long life, and the city was also called Graia for a long period. Homer used Graia as the city's name in his Catalogue.

l: Triton at Tanagra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Triton at Tanagra is a figure represented by a notable statue at the temple of Dionysus. Said to attack women, ambush herds, and plunder vessels, he is defeated after drinking wine, falling asleep, and being beheaded by a man of Tanagra.

l: statue of Triton, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The statue of Triton in the temple of Dionysus is especially wonderful, even more wonderful than Dionysus’s statue; it lacks a head, said to have been struck off by a man of Tanagra with an axe.

l: women of Tanagra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: perform women's bathing in the sea [before the orgies of Dionysus, according to an ancient legend] Before the orgies of Dionysus, the women of Tanagra bathed in the sea to purify themselves. Triton attacked them while they were swimming, and they prayed to Dionysus for help.

l: women's bathing in the sea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: precedes orgies of Dionysus [as a purification rite] The women of Tanagra bathed in the sea before the orgies of Dionysus in order to purify themselves.

l: Triton's assault on the women, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_an_attack_on women of Tanagra [while they were swimming in the sea] Triton assaulted the women of Tanagra while they were swimming in the sea after bathing to purify themselves. They prayed to Dionysus for aid.

l: fight between Dionysus and Triton, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a fight [in which Dionysus conquered Triton] According to an ancient legend, Dionysus answered the women's prayer and fought Triton. Dionysus conquered Triton.

l: Triton's ambush of the herds, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: According to a more plausible but less ancient legend, Triton lay in ambush when herds were driven to the sea and carried some of them off. He also plundered small vessels.

l: killing of Triton, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_carried_out_by man of Tanagra [with an axe] In one account, the people of Tanagra filled a bowl with wine for Triton, and he drank it, fell asleep, and tumbled down the rocks. A man of Tanagra then struck off his head with an axe; because Triton was captured while drunk, they thought he was killed by Dionysus.

l: Ethiopian bulls, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ethiopian bulls are rhinoceroses, named for one projecting nose horn and a smaller horn beneath it; they have no horns on their heads.

l: rhinoceroses, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a name for Ethiopian bulls The name rhinoceroses is applied to the Ethiopian bulls because they have a horn projecting from the nose and another smaller horn beneath it, while lacking horns on the head.

l: elk, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The elk is a wild animal found among the Celts, resembling both a stag and a camel. It scents men from far away and hides in rocks and cave recesses, making it hard to hunt or see at a distance. It is occasionally captured when a large net encloses its area.

l: tiger, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tiger is a wild animal identified with Ctesias's Indian martiora, called manslayer by the Greeks. Reports of three rows of teeth and tail stings are rejected. Its apparently uniform red color, often seen in sunlight, is explained as an effect of sunlight, speed, or constant motion.

l: Indians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Indians are said to report that the tiger has three rows of teeth in each jaw and a tail with stings that it can hurl at a distance. The speaker believes they accept this account because of their excessive terror of the animal and says they are also mistaken about its color.

l: wild animals, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: vary_by_region different forms [across Libya, India, Arabia, and Greece] Wild animals differ between climates and lands, so animals found in remote Libya, India, or Arabia would not necessarily be the same as those found in Greece. Their appearance and kinds are presented as subject to the conditions of different regions.

l: Anthedon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Anthedon is a Boeotian city on the sea at the foot of Messapium, named after Nymph Anthedon according to one account; it contains sacred sites, tombs, and the leap of Glaucus.

l: Cabiri, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cabiri are former inhabitants of a town at the sanctuary site, driven out by Argives after Thebes fell; Telondes and others later returned when mysteries were restored, and they punish unauthorized imitators implacably.

l: Iphimedea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Iphimedea, from Arcadia, appears near Eurynomus in a painting and is greatly honoured by Carians at Mylasa.

l: Glaucus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Glaucus begins as a fisherman, then becomes a marine god after eating transforming grass. Especially seafaring men believe he predicts the future; Pindar and Aeschylus celebrated him, and Aeschylus made him a play’s subject.

l: tomb of Pindar, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The tomb of Pindar is situated in the Hippodrome near the race-course of Iolaus.

l: Acræphnium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Acræphnium, originally a city in the district of Thebes, stands on Mount Ptoum, has a notable temple and statue of Dionysus, and received Theban refugees after Thebes’ destruction.

l: Ptoan Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ptoan Apollo was worshipped at a temple about fifteen stades from Acræphnium, had an oracle before Alexander and the Macedonians invaded and Thebes was destroyed, and was linked to Ptous.

l: temple of Ptoan Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Ptoan Apollo stood about fifteen stades beyond Acræphnium on Mount Ptoum. Before Alexander's invasion and the destruction of Thebes, it was associated with an infallible oracle.

l: oracle of Ptoan Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The oracle of Ptoan Apollo, once considered infallible before invasion and destruction, answered Mys’s consultation in Carian rather than Greek.

l: Larymna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Larymna is a Boeotian coastal city, named after Larymna, daughter of Cynus. Formerly reckoned with Opus, its inhabitants voluntarily joined the Boeotians when the Thebans became powerful. It has a deep harbour, a temple and standing statue of Dionysus, and mountains above it for wild-boar hunting.

l: lake Cephisis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lake Cephisis, also called Copais by some, receives the rivers Cephisus and Melas and covers much of the Orchomenian district. In winter, when the South Wind generally prevails, it spreads over most of the country. Nearby towns, including Athenæ and Eleusis, were said by the Bœotians to have been swept away by a winter flood. Its eels are especially fine to eat.

l: Cephisus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cephisus is a river rising at Lilæa in Phocis and flowing into Lake Cephisis; Thebans said Hercules diverted it into the Orchomenian plain and blocked its sea outlet.
